A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EscapeBench benchmark and EscapeAgent framework. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite retitling and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original model and human evaluations on EscapeBench, supplemented by case studies, error analyses and Appendix D results.

after.justification: The original evaluations remain, with additional model comparisons, module ablations, participant-survey results and automatic-annotation examples in Section 6 and Appendices E–F.

M1.justification: The game engine, action space, BaseAgent, Reflection task-list operations and Foresight triggers remain unchanged, including the procedures and prompts in Appendix C. The new component-disabled variants are ablation conditions, not revisions to the proposed full agent.

E1.justification: Both retain the same 12 escape-room scenarios and 36 difficulty settings. Additional model variants and participant characterization do not establish new benchmark tasks or populations; Appendix F expands the previously mentioned automatic-annotation investigation.

E2.justification: Tables 6–7 add Qwen-2.5-Coder/Math-7B comparisons and Reflection-only/Foresight-only variants; Section 6.1 also identifies Llama-3.2-1B/3B evaluations. Conversely, Qwen2.5-72B disappears from the cumulative-completion comparison in v1 Figure 9 versus v2 Figure 6, although its table results remain.

E3.justification: The main 36-setting evaluation, 50-action hint trigger, 10-step memory and metrics remain unchanged. New module ablations compare four agent configurations on all scenarios at normal difficulty using GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-70B. Appendix E introduces a post-experiment participant survey; this does not establish a change to the original human gameplay protocol.

E4.justification: Section 6 adds controlled tests of the individual Foresight and Reflection contributions and diagnostics of model scale and specialization. Appendix E analyzes participant experience, while Appendix F expands annotation-failure analysis with generated examples. Earlier difficulty, error and progress analyses largely remain, often relocated.

E5.justification: Both retain sampling settings T=0 and n=1 and report point results without repeated-run uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals. Appendix E asserts no significant performance difference between participant groups but specifies no statistical test or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Retained model and human scores in Tables 3 and 5 are identical, but Tables 6–7 add specialist-model and component-ablation results. For example, the new normal-difficulty GPT-4o comparison reports 5.00 hints and 452.00 steps for EscapeAgent versus 9.83 and 707.33 for BaseAgent. Appendices E–F add survey and annotation findings, while Qwen2.5-72B cumulative-completion curves are removed. These are additional or removed results, not improvements to the original aggregate scores.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces formal theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. The discussion of theoretical foundations for creativity is conceptual and largely retained through relocation to Appendix G.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: EscapeBench evaluates creative agent reasoning, EscapeAgent combines Foresight and Reflection, and current models remain behind humans despite reduced hint and step requirements. Retitling and condensation do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning module complementarity, Foresight's dependence on the task list, specialization-related limitations and minimum useful model scale. Appendices E–F additionally argue for the human baseline's representativeness and explain limits of automated puzzle creation. The new assertion that the full agent consistently performs best overstates Table 7, where individual-module variants sometimes achieve higher early-exit progress.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly discloses an automated annotation checker and manual cross-validation, while Appendix E provides the participant-survey questions. Existing agent prompts, hardware, inference framework, resource estimates and code link remain substantively unchanged. These additions document procedures without establishing changes to the original implementation.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including ToolRL, OTC, ModelingAgent, EmbodiedBench and MultiAgentBench, and removes MEMORYLLM and two human-robot creativity references. The central positioning against goal-oriented agent benchmarks remains unchanged; other bibliography edits mainly concern formatting or metadata.

P1.justification: The title changes, and substantial portions of the introduction, benchmark construction, method explanation and discussion are condensed or rewritten. The separate motivation subsection is absorbed into Section 3, analyses are reorganized, and detailed future directions move to Appendix G. New analysis, ethics and appendix sections further reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: Figures and tables are extensively regrouped and resized, and Tables 6–7 are added. V1 Figures 5, 6 and 10 move to the appendix as v2 Figures 12–14; progress-interval panels are redistributed between the main text and appendix. The cumulative-completion plot drops Qwen curves and revises its axes and legend. Table 3 replaces the oracle row with its average step count in the caption.

improvement.justification: The new controlled ablations address v1's lack of evidence separating Foresight and Reflection and support their combined benefit on the primary hint and step metrics. Human-survey and annotation details also improve transparency. These gains are limited by missing survey sample-size/test details and an overstatement of ablation superiority: Table 7 reports GPT-4o early-exit progress of 44.55% for the full agent versus 48.89% with Foresight alone.
